details_explanation.topic: Third conditional, inverted conditionals, past perfect
details_explanation.sample: Had I known about the risks, I would never have agreed to the plan.
details_explanation.id: Seandainya saya tahu tentang risikonya, saya tidak akan pernah menyetujui rencana itu.
details_explanation.explanation: The if-clause of a third conditional uses the past perfect ('had known'), never 'would have known'. Inversion ('Had I known') is an acceptable formal alternative that omits 'if'. 'If I had been aware' and 'Had I been aware' are also acceptable paraphrases.
details_explanation.introduction: Third conditionals describe unreal past situations. The if-clause takes the past perfect; the main clause takes 'would have + past participle'. Inversion can replace 'if' in formal registers.

rules.title: 1. Standard third conditional
rules.explanation: Use past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.
rules.structure: If + past perfect, subject + would have + past participle
notes: If I had known, I would have acted differently.
Never 'If I would have known'.

rules.title: 2. Inverted conditional
rules.explanation: Drop 'if' and invert auxiliary and subject for a formal alternative.
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle
notes: Had I known, I would have acted differently.
Had she been aware, she would have objected.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have helped.
common_mistakes.correct: If I had known, I would have helped.
common_mistakes.reason: Do not use 'would have' in the if-clause.

details_explanation.topic: Passive voice, gerund vs. infinitive after 'need/require', non-defining relative clauses
details_explanation.sample: The old theatre needs to be renovated before it can reopen.
details_explanation.id: Teater tua itu perlu direnovasi sebelum dapat dibuka kembali.
details_explanation.explanation: After 'need' and 'require', use either 'to be + past participle' or the gerund. 'Needs to being restored' is ungrammatical because 'to' must be followed by the base form. Acceptable: 'needs to be restored', 'needs restoring', 'requires restoring', 'requires to be restored'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Need' and 'require' can take a passive infinitive or a gerund with passive meaning.

rules.title: 1. need/require + to be + past participle
rules.structure: need/require + to be + past participle
notes: The bridge needs to be restored.
The report requires to be checked.

rules.title: 2. need/require + gerund
rules.structure: need/require + verb-ing
notes: The bridge needs restoring.
The report requires checking.

common_mistakes.wrong: The bridge needs to being restored.
common_mistakes.correct: The bridge needs to be restored.
common_mistakes.reason: 'To' must be followed by the base form 'be'.

details_explanation.topic: Subjunctive mood after 'insist', reported speech, inversion after 'not until'
details_explanation.sample: The committee insisted that he resign immediately.
details_explanation.id: Komite menuntut agar dia segera mengundurkan diri.
details_explanation.explanation: After verbs of demand such as 'insist', 'demand', 'request', 'suggest', the that-clause takes the base form (subjunctive) in formal English. 'Submits' must become 'submit' (or 'should submit', 'must submit', 'was to submit' as acceptable paraphrases). The passage also illustrates inversion after 'not until', which is correctly formed.
details_explanation.introduction: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing demand, suggestion, or request. It uses the base form of the verb regardless of the subject.

rules.title: 1. Subjunctive after 'insist'
rules.explanation: Use the base form in the that-clause.
rules.structure: insist that + subject + base verb
notes: They insisted that he leave.
She insisted that the report be submitted.

rules.title: 2. Inversion after 'not until'
rules.explanation: When 'not until' begins a clause, the main clause is inverted.
rules.structure: Not until + clause + auxiliary + subject + verb
notes: Not until he apologized did she speak to him.
Not until then did we realize the danger.

common_mistakes.wrong: They insisted that he leaves.
common_mistakes.correct: They insisted that he leave.
common_mistakes.reason: The subjunctive uses the base form.

details_explanation.topic: Relative clauses, subject-verb agreement with 'the number of', present perfect vs. past simple
details_explanation.sample: The number of students who have registered has risen sharply.
details_explanation.id: Jumlah siswa yang telah mendaftar telah meningkat tajam.
details_explanation.explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'applicants' (plural), so the relative-clause verb must be plural: 'who have submitted' (or 'that have submitted', 'who submitted', 'that submitted', 'who had submitted'). Note that the main verb 'have increased' is also wrong—it should be 'has increased' because the main subject is 'the number' (singular). Only the relative-clause error is clickable here; however, in a full correction both must be fixed.
details_explanation.introduction: Relative clauses agree with their antecedent. 'The number of' takes a singular main verb, while the relative pronoun inside the phrase agrees with the plural noun it modifies.

rules.title: 1. Relative clause agreement
rules.explanation: The verb in the relative clause agrees with the antecedent.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + who/that + plural verb
notes: The number of students who have applied is rising.
The number of cars that were sold has doubled.

rules.title: 2. Main verb agreement
rules.explanation: The main subject is 'the number', which is singular.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + singular main verb
notes: The number of applicants has increased.
The number of issues is growing.

common_mistakes.wrong: The number of applicants who has submitted have increased.
common_mistakes.correct: The number of applicants who have submitted has increased.
common_mistakes.reason: Relative verb agrees with 'applicants'; main verb agrees with 'number'.

details_explanation.topic: Modal perfect, past participle forms, third conditional implications
details_explanation.sample: You should have gone over the figures before submitting.
details_explanation.id: Anda seharusnya memeriksa angka-angka itu sebelum menyerahkan.
details_explanation.explanation: After a modal perfect ('should have', 'ought to have', 'must have'), the main verb must be a past participle, not the past simple. 'Went' is the past simple of 'go'; the correct past participle is 'gone'. Acceptable corrections include 'should have gone', 'ought to have gone', 'should have left', 'ought to have left', 'must have gone' (depending on the intended nuance).
details_explanation.introduction: Modal perfects express speculation, regret, or obligation about the past. They are formed with modal + have + past participle.

rules.title: 1. Modal + have + past participle
rules.explanation: Never use the past simple after 'have' in a modal perfect.
rules.structure: modal + have + past participle
notes: She should have gone.
They must have left.

rules.title: 2. Past participle vs. past simple
rules.structure: go–went–gone; see–saw–seen; take–took–taken
notes: He should have seen it.
They ought to have taken action.

common_mistakes.wrong: She should have went.
common_mistakes.correct: She should have gone.

other_examples.sentence: They ought to have informed us earlier.
other_examples.translation: Mereka seharusnya memberi tahu kami lebih awal.

other_examples.sentence: He must have forgotten the appointment.
other_examples.translation: Dia pasti lupa janji temu itu.

details_explanation.topic: Gerund after preposition, phrasal verbs with 'to', future forms
details_explanation.sample: I look forward to hearing from you.
details_explanation.id: Saya menantikan kabar dari Anda.
details_explanation.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so it must be followed by a gerund (-ing form). 'To meet' is therefore wrong. Acceptable: 'to meeting you', 'to meeting with you', 'to seeing you', 'to meeting up with you'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some expressions ending in 'to' contain a preposition, not an infinitive. These include 'look forward to', 'be used to', 'object to', 'in addition to', and 'devote oneself to'.

rules.title: 1. Preposition 'to' + gerund
rules.explanation: When 'to' is a preposition, use the -ing form.
rules.structure: look forward to + verb-ing
notes: I look forward to meeting you.
She is used to working late.

rules.title: 2. Infinitive 'to' + base verb
rules.explanation: When 'to' is an infinitive marker, use the base form.
rules.structure: want/need/hope + to + base verb
notes: I want to meet you.
She hopes to work late.

common_mistakes.wrong: I look forward to meet you.
common_mistakes.correct: I look forward to meeting you.

details_explanation.topic: Inversion after 'not only', correlative conjunctions, past perfect passive
details_explanation.sample: Not only was he late, but he also forgot the documents.
details_explanation.id: Bukan hanya dia terlambat, tetapi dia juga lupa dokumen-dokumen itu.
details_explanation.explanation: When a sentence begins with 'not only', the subject and auxiliary in the first clause must be inverted. 'He was late' therefore becomes 'was he late'. Acceptable: 'was he late', 'had he been late', 'did he arrive late', 'was he delayed'.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative adverbials at the start of a clause trigger subject–auxiliary inversion.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after 'not only'
rules.explanation: Place the auxiliary before the subject.
rules.structure: Not only + auxiliary + subject + main verb
notes: Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Not only was he late, but he also forgot.

rules.title: 2. Other negative adverbials
rules.explanation: The same rule applies to 'never', 'rarely', 'seldom', 'hardly', 'no sooner', and 'not until'.
rules.structure: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + verb
notes: Never have I seen such a thing.
Rarely does he complain.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not only he was late, but he also forgot.
common_mistakes.correct: Not only was he late, but he also forgot.
common_mistakes.reason: Invert subject and auxiliary after 'not only'.

details_explanation.topic: Subjunctive mood after 'recommend', passive voice, time clauses
details_explanation.sample: The professor recommended that the thesis be revised before submission.
details_explanation.id: Profesor merekomendasikan agar tesis itu direvisi sebelum diserahkan.
details_explanation.explanation: After 'recommend' (like 'suggest', 'insist', 'demand'), the that-clause takes the base form of the verb. In the passive this becomes 'be + past participle'. Acceptable: 'be revised', 'should be revised', 'was revised' (informal), 'gets revised' (informal).
details_explanation.introduction: The subjunctive is used after verbs of suggestion and recommendation, especially in formal English.

rules.title: 1. Active subjunctive
rules.explanation: Use the base form regardless of subject.
rules.structure: recommend that + subject + base verb
notes: She recommended that he apply.
They suggested that we wait.

rules.title: 2. Passive subjunctive
rules.structure: recommend that + subject + be + past participle
notes: She recommended that the report be revised.
They suggested that the policy be reviewed.

common_mistakes.wrong: The professor recommended that the thesis is revised.

common_mistakes.reason: The subjunctive uses the base form.

details_explanation.topic: Third conditional, inversion, modal substitutes ('be able to', 'could'), non-defining relative clauses
details_explanation.sample: Had the warning been issued earlier, they would have been able to evacuate.
details_explanation.id: Seandainya peringatan dikeluarkan lebih awal, mereka akan mampu mengungsi.
details_explanation.explanation: The first part is a correct inverted third conditional. The error lies in the relative clause: 'couldn't do' is vague and stylistically weak. Acceptable refinements include 'which they were unable to do', 'which they had not been able to do', 'which was not possible', 'which proved impossible'.
details_explanation.introduction: Third conditionals can be inverted with 'Had'. 'Be able to' is a common substitute for 'can/could' in perfect and future contexts.

rules.title: 1. Inverted third conditional
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle
notes: Had they known, they would have acted.
Had the warning been issued, they would have evacuated.

rules.title: 2. Ability in the past perfect
rules.explanation: 'Could' has no perfect form; use 'had been able to' or 'were unable to'.
rules.structure: had been able to / were unable to + verb
notes: They had been able to evacuate.
They were unable to evacuate.

common_mistakes.wrong: They couldn't have been able to evacuate.
common_mistakes.correct: They had not been able to evacuate.
common_mistakes.reason: Avoid double modals; use 'be able to'.

details_explanation.topic: Past subjunctive after 'it is high time', present perfect continuous, collective nouns
details_explanation.sample: It is high time they made a decision.
details_explanation.id: Sudah waktunya mereka mengambil keputusan.
details_explanation.explanation: After 'it is high time', the following clause uses the past simple (or 'should + base verb') to express urgency. 'They make' is therefore wrong. Acceptable: 'they made', 'they should make', 'they were to make', 'a decision was made'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'It is high time', 'it is about time', and 'it is time' are followed by the past subjunctive or 'should + base verb'.

rules.title: 1. It is high time + past simple
rules.explanation: The past form signals urgency or criticism.
rules.structure: It is high time + subject + past simple
notes: It is high time you left.
It is high time we took action.

rules.title: 2. It is high time + should + base verb
rules.structure: It is high time + subject + should + base verb
notes: It is high time you should leave.
It is high time we should act.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is high time they make a decision.
common_mistakes.correct: It is high time they made a decision.
common_mistakes.reason: Use the past simple after 'it is high time'.

details_explanation.topic: Relative clauses ('which' vs. 'what'), non-defining clauses, result connectors
details_explanation.sample: The report is incomplete, which has caused frustration.
details_explanation.id: Laporan itu belum selesai, yang telah menimbulkan frustrasi.
details_explanation.explanation: 'What' cannot be used as a relative pronoun referring back to a whole clause. The correct connector is 'which' (non-defining relative), or a coordinating/result connector such as 'and this', 'thereby', etc. Acceptable: 'which has caused', 'which caused', 'and this has caused', 'thereby causing'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Which' can refer to a whole previous clause in non-defining relative clauses; 'what' cannot.

rules.title: 1. 'Which' referring to a clause
rules.explanation: Use 'which' to comment on the whole preceding clause.
rules.structure: ..., which + verb ...
notes: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.
The report is late, which is unacceptable.

rules.title: 2. 'What' as a fused relative
rules.explanation: 'What' means 'the thing that' and cannot refer back to a clause.
rules.structure: What + clause + verb
notes: What he said was true.
What happened next surprised us.

common_mistakes.wrong: He was late, what annoyed everyone.
common_mistakes.correct: He was late, which annoyed everyone.
common_mistakes.reason: Use 'which', not 'what', to refer to a clause.

details_explanation.topic: Neither…nor (proximity rule), collective nouns, result clauses
details_explanation.sample: Neither the CEO nor the board members were willing to compromise.
details_explanation.id: Baik CEO maupun anggota dewan tidak bersedia berkompromi.
details_explanation.explanation: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Board members' is plural and closer, so 'was willing' must be 'were willing'. Acceptable: 'were willing', 'were prepared', 'were ready', 'were inclined'.
details_explanation.introduction: In 'neither … nor' constructions, the verb follows the proximity rule and agrees with the closest subject.

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule
rules.explanation: Verb agrees with the nearer subject.
rules.structure: Neither S1 nor S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: Neither the manager nor the employees were present.
Neither the employees nor the manager was present.

rules.title: 2. Collective noun caution
rules.explanation: If one subject is a collective noun, its number depends on whether it acts as a unit.
rules.structure: Collective noun + singular/plural verb depending on context
notes: The board was united.
The board were divided.

details_explanation.topic: Existential 'there', subject–verb agreement with plural nouns, 'data' as plural, reported speech
details_explanation.sample: The data suggest that there are significant discrepancies.
details_explanation.id: Data tersebut menunjukkan bahwa ada perbedaan signifikan.
details_explanation.explanation: In the existential construction 'there is/are', the verb agrees with the noun phrase following it. 'Significant discrepancies' is plural, so 'is' must become 'are'. Acceptable: 'there are', 'there were', 'there exist', 'there remain'. Note that 'data' is treated as plural in formal academic English, so 'suggest' is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Existential 'there' is not the grammatical subject; agreement follows the notional subject.

rules.title: 1. There is + singular / There are + plural
rules.structure: There is + singular; There are + plural
notes: There is a problem.
There are several problems.

rules.title: 2. Data as plural in academic register
rules.structure: The data + plural verb
notes: The data suggest a trend.
The data are conclusive.

common_mistakes.wrong: The data suggests that there is discrepancies.
common_mistakes.correct: The data suggest that there are discrepancies.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Data' is plural in formal English; 'discrepancies' is plural.

details_explanation.topic: Concession clauses ('despite' vs. 'although'), gerund after preposition, past perfect
details_explanation.sample: Despite having worked overtime, they could not finish.
details_explanation.id: Meskipun telah bekerja lembur, mereka tidak dapat menyelesaikannya.
details_explanation.explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition and must be followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund—not by a full clause. 'Despite they had worked' is therefore ungrammatical. Acceptable: 'despite having worked', 'despite the fact that they had worked', 'although they had worked', 'even though they had worked'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Despite/In spite of' take a noun or gerund; 'although/even though' take a clause.

rules.structure: despite + noun/-ing
notes: Despite the rain, we went out.
Despite having worked hard, he failed.

rules.title: 2. Although + clause

notes: Although it rained, we went out.

details_explanation.topic: Articles ('a' vs. 'an'), inversion after 'scarcely', participle clauses
details_explanation.sample: They evacuated the building in an orderly manner.
details_explanation.id: Mereka mengevakuasi gedung itu secara tertib.
details_explanation.explanation: The article 'an' is required before a vowel sound. 'Orderly' begins with a vowel sound /ɔː/, so 'a orderly' is wrong. Acceptable: 'in an orderly manner', 'in an orderly fashion', 'in an organized manner', 'in an organized fashion'. Note the passage also correctly uses inversion after 'scarcely'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'A' is used before consonant sounds, 'an' before vowel sounds.

rules.title: 1. A vs. An
rules.explanation: Base the choice on the sound, not the letter.
rules.structure: a + consonant sound; an + vowel sound
notes: a university (consonant sound /juː/)
an hour (silent h)
an orderly manner

rules.title: 2. Inversion after 'scarcely'
rules.explanation: 'Scarcely … when' requires inversion in the first clause.
rules.structure: Scarcely + auxiliary + subject + past participle + when …
notes: Scarcely had he arrived when the phone rang.
Scarcely had we sat down when the show began.

details_explanation.topic: Subjunctive after 'require that', non-defining relative clauses, future time clauses
details_explanation.sample: The rules require that every employee complete the training.
details_explanation.id: Aturan-aturan itu mewajibkan setiap karyawan menyelesaikan pelatihan.
details_explanation.explanation: 'Require that' takes the subjunctive: the verb in the that-clause appears in its base form. 'Completes' should therefore be 'complete'. Acceptable: 'complete', 'should complete', 'must complete', 'are to complete'.
details_explanation.introduction: Verbs such as 'require', 'request', 'demand', 'insist', 'suggest', and 'recommend' can take a subjunctive that-clause.

rules.title: 1. Subjunctive after 'require'
rules.explanation: Use the base form regardless of subject.
rules.structure: require that + subject + base verb
notes: They require that he be present.
The law requires that everyone register.

rules.title: 2. Formal alternatives
rules.explanation: 'Should' or modal paraphrases also occur, especially in British English.
rules.structure: require that + subject + should + base verb
notes: They require that he should be present.
The law requires that everyone should register.

common_mistakes.wrong: The rules require that every employee completes the training.
